newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand readies for bitter IMF economic pill.
newsitem.headline: Thailand readies for bitter IMF economic pill.

text.p: Thailand is preparing for the bitter pill of a tough austerity package to be prescribed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and his beleaguered economic team this week laid the groundwork for the package following turmoil in the financial, property and business sectors that led to a de facto devaluation of the baht four weeks ago.
Analysts on Wednesday urged Chavalit to embrace an economic package being negotiated with the IMF, saying it was needed to restore confidence in the baht and the economy.
"The government must not show the slightest hesitation in accepting IMF conditions if it wants to regain market confidence," said Banluesak Pussarangsi, chief analyst of The Mutual Fund Plc.
Analysts said Chavalit needed to display courage in the months ahead by ignoring resistance in his six-party coalition government to additional national budget cuts.

They said the IMF package would seek hefty budget cuts to narrow the widening Thai balance of payment deficit, which has been aggravated by capital outflows and defence of the baht in the currency markets in recent months.
The May balance of payments deficit widened to 112.3 billion baht from 15.5 billion in April.
"I think politicians would appreciate by now that they have no choice but to sacrifice their budgets for national interest," said Vuth Puthamon of Multi-Credit Corp of Thailand Plc.
The Thai economy, hit by weak exports and a property sector slump, is seen growing at its slowest pace in over a decade.
The bursting of the Thai economic bubble is set to produce the first government budget deficit since the mid-1980s in the 1996/1997 and 1997/1998 (October-September) fiscal years.

The baht depreciation of over 20 percent since July 2 has nearly crippled the private sector, which has seen its $60 billion of foreign debt balloon. Thai borrowers have also seen their credit lines cut by wary foreign creditors.
Thira Ashakul of the Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand rated the task of reversing the recent capital flight as the most pressing job facing Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya.
He said Thanong needed to move fast to contain looming corporate bankruptcies, especially in the troubled 91-company finance sector which has been hit hard by a liquidity crunch.

Thanong has said he plans to unveil a comprehensive economic reform package, that may include a standby credit line from the IMF, by August 5. He declined to say how much Thailand would seek to borrow from the IMF but analysts say the figure may be $10 billion,
Analysts said the government had failed to issue clear guidelines for bailing out 16 cash-strapped finance and securities firms that were suspended from doing new business last month.

The 16 companies, with combined 400 billion baht ($13 billion) assets last March, would have their books audited by the government in the next two months. They would also be helped by the government to merge with stronger firms within a year.

"Under IMF guidance, these firms would probably need to write off their losses before the government injects taxpayers' money to bail them out. Any firm refusing that requirement should be allowed to fold if necessary," Vuth of MCC said.

Banluesak of Mutual Fund said the market was not convinced of the viability of the government's finance sector bailout plan until the authorities set clear, systematic guidelines on how Thai and foreign investors could help revive the sector.
Analysts said another distasteful pill from the IMF could be an expected requirement for the government to curb subsidies to state-run utilities.

They said that although higher utility charges and an expected value added tax (VAT) hike to about 10 percent may further stoke inflation, they would curb consumer spending and strengthen the economy in the long term.
Thailand currently levies VAT at seven percent and inflation runs at around 4.3 percent.
Some analysts believe the IMF would recommend that Thailand cut public spending, particularly in areas such as defence, instead of raising taxes.
